newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Taiwan's Lee off key as Asia sings Deng's praises.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan's Lee off key as Asia sings Deng's praises.

text.p: Asian leaders and media on Friday sounded more glowing tributes to Chinese patriarch Deng Xiaoping but Taiwanese President Lee Teng-hui struck a discordant note, saying the island had weathered worse storms.
"We should not take this issue too seriously," Lee was quoted as having told a group of national assemblymen on Thursday.
Deng, 92, died on late on Wednesday of respiratory failure and was in the advanced stages of Parkinson's disease.

"We have experienced the most dangerous missile crisis, so we should have confidence and not become unravelled," the Central Daily News newspaper, owned by the ruling Nationalist Party, quoted Lee as saying.
He was referring to missile tests China conducted off Taiwan in March last year, designed to intimidate Taipei ahead of its presidential election that month.
Elsewhere, Singapore elder statesman Lee Kuan Yew said Deng's spirit and courage never failed, and he helped set the stage for China to become a heavyweight nation.

"He saved China. Without him, China could have been like the Soviet Union. Instead China will become a huge heavyweight nation in 30 years," Lee said in a letter to Chinese President Jiang Zemin released late on Thursday.

The Straits Times echoed this view, saying Deng was "one of the great men of the 20th century" and could one day be judged "China's most inspired leader" despite his 1989 crackdown on pro-democracy activists in Tiananmen Square.
Vietnam's top leaders, in their first comment on the death of a man once considered a mortal enemy, sent a message to Beijing describing Deng's death as a loss for China.
The statement, carried in Friday's official press, expressed sympathy and said Deng had made important contributions to the development of China and to its economic and social opening.
"The death of Comrade Deng Xiaoping is a great loss to the Communist Party and the people of China," the statement said.
But there was no mention of his role in relations between the two socialist neighbours, who fought a 1979 border war which was followed by a lengthy period of frontier hostilities.

The Philippine Star newspaper hailed Deng for setting free the Chinese entrepreneurial spirit which transformed the world's most populous nation from an Asian backwater to an emerging economic powerhouse.

Beijing's communist hardliners were unlikely to tinker with a formula that has worked to give 1.5 billion Chinese economic stability for the past several years, the Star editorial said, adding: "Part of Deng's legacy is that he left Beijing's hardliners with little choice but to sustain his reforms."
In Thailand, The Bangkok Post said Deng would be remembered as the architect who liberalised China's economy and enabled it to become a member of the international community.

"But despite all his achievements on the economic front, Deng's legacy is stained with blood by his decision to brutally stamp out pro-democracy demonstrations in Tiananmen Square in 1989 and the subsequent crackdown on dissidents since then," the Post's editorial said.

The Nation, another English-language daily, said in its editorial that the 15th party congress in October would be crucial for Jiang, where Prime Minister Li Peng was expected to step down and a new prime minister-designate named.
